finding.claim: sync() sends a server-side GET to an unvalidated, client-supplied iconUrl, enabling blind SSRF to arbitrary http/https targets.
finding.source: icon parameter of update(String webhook, String icon) reached via PUT /profile (src/Profile.java:10-11)

trace.note: update() accepts icon from the PUT /profile request
this.iconUrl = icon; stored with no validation
sync(HttpClient c) runs as the nightly job
server issues GET and reads the body into a byte array

finding.guards_checked: No scheme, host, IP-range, or port check on icon (src/Profile.java:11-16, 23). HttpClient is injected, so its redirect policy is not visible; java.net.http defaults to no redirects. Only http/https schemes are possible, so file: is not reachable. Response body is discarded, so the SSRF is blind. Whether PUT /profile requires auth is not visible in this repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only validation is on webhook at src/Profile.java:12-14, and icon is stored unchecked at line 16. sync() passes iconUrl straight to URI.create and c.send at lines 23-24 with no scheme, host, or IP check.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: update() stores the client-supplied icon unvalidated at src/Profile.java:16, and sync() issues a server-side GET to it at lines 23-24. The value is attacker-controlled because it comes from the PUT /profile request, which is a user-level endpoint, and no closing guard exists. Whether the endpoint requires auth is not visible in this repo, but even authenticated low-privilege users can set it, so the finding stands.
